body.text: This page explains the IRS Form 6765 instructions for the 2024 tax year, which apply to U.S. taxpayers claiming the research credit under IRC Section 41. The revised form makes Item A, Item B, Section E, and Section F mandatory for 2024, while Section G business component reporting remains optional on original returns through the 2025 tax year.
Executive Summary: The 2024–2025 Regulatory Overhaul of Form 6765

The Internal Revenue Service (IRS) instituted a comprehensive structural revision to Form 6765, Credit for Increasing Research Activities (Rev. December 2024), and its accompanying Instructions for Form 6765 (Rev. January 2025, subsequently clarified on June 18, 2025, and updated in December 2025), applicable beginning with the 2024 tax year. Finalized after multiple rounds of external stakeholder feedback on preliminary previews and draft versions released in 2023 and June 2024 (including IRS News Release IR-2024-171), the revised Form 6765 represents a fundamental shift in how research credit claims under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 41 are reported, substantiated, and evaluated for examination risk. The IRS articulated three primary administrative objectives for overhauling the form and its instructions: establishing greater consistency in tax reporting across diverse taxpayers and industries, elevating the quality and granularity of project-level information gathered for effective tax administration, and enabling more efficient agency resource allocation and upfront return risk assessment.

Prior versions of Form 6765 permitted taxpayers to report Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) strictly as entity-level aggregates across wages, supplies, computer rental or lease costs, and contract research, leaving project-level substantiation and business-component nexus to post-filing examination Information Document Requests (IDRs) or amended return attachments. The revised Form 6765 (Rev. December 2024) dismantles that high-level aggregation model by introducing new front-page header elections and three major structural sections across the filing architecture. At the top header of Page 1, Item A relocates the irrevocable IRC Section 280C reduced credit election from its former embedded placement in Sections A and B to a mandatory front-page binary ("Yes"/"No") indicator, while Item B introduces a mandatory front-page binary ("Yes"/"No") controlled group disclosure requiring explicit confirmation of whether the claimant belongs to a controlled group of corporations or group of trades or businesses under common control, accompanied by a standardized group allocation attachment (Form6765ItemBGroupCredit.pdf).

In the body of the return, Section E (Other Information, Lines 37 through 41) establishes mandatory quantitative and qualitative disclosures for all claimants reporting QREs on Line 48, capturing the total number of qualifying business components generating QREs, the exact dollar amount of corporate officers' wages included in QREs, binary indicators for trade or business acquisitions or dispositions and newly identified QRE categories, and reliance on the Large Business & International (LB&I) ASC 730 Financial Statement R&D Directive. Furthermore, Section F (Qualified Research Expenses Summary, Question A and Lines 42 through 48) centralizes and standardizes the consolidation of total QREs across in-house qualified wages, supplies, computer rental or lease costs, contract research expenses, and basic research payments on Line 48 prior to computing the credit in Section A (Line 5) or Section B (Line 20). Finally, Section G (Business Component Information, Columns 49(a) through 56) mandates the disaggregated qualitative identification and quantitative cost allocation of QREs on a project-by-project (business component) basis under the "80%/Top 50" reporting threshold.

To provide taxpayers adequate lead time to reconfigure internal cost-accounting, general ledger, and engineering project-tracking infrastructures, the IRS established a phased transition schedule. Under the initial Instructions for Form 6765 (Rev. January 2025), the IRS made Section G optional for all filers for tax years beginning before 2025 (the 2024 tax year) and scheduled Section G to become mandatory for tax years beginning after 2024 (the 2025 tax year), subject to statutory and administrative exemptions for qualified small businesses electing the payroll tax credit and eligible smaller claimants. In subsequent administrative guidance (IR-2025-99 and the December 2025 update to the Instructions for Form 6765), the IRS extended the optional transition period by one additional year so that Section G remains optional for all original return filers for tax years beginning before 2026 (covering both the 2024 and 2025 tax years) and becomes mandatory for tax years beginning after 2025 (the 2026 tax year), while maintaining mandatory business-component disclosure rules for amended return refund claims. Consequently, the 2024 Form 6765 instructions function both as the binding compliance rulebook for 2024 tax returns—where Header Items A and B, Section E, and Section F are immediately mandatory—and as the operational blueprint for mandatory business-component reporting under Section G.

body.text: Statutory Foundations and QRE Quantification Rules on Form 6765
IRC Section 41 Scope and Business Component Definition

The federal Research and Development (R&D) tax credit under IRC Section 41 incentivizes domestic research expenditures paid or incurred in carrying on a trade or business to develop new or improved business components. Under IRC Section 41(d)(2)(B), Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4(b)(1), and the Instructions for Form 6765, a business component is statutorily defined as any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention which is to be held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in a trade or business of the taxpayer. Furthermore, under IRC Section 41(d)(2)(C), any plant process, machinery, or technique for commercial production of a business component is treated as a separate business component from the product being produced, meaning research relating to the development of a manufacturing process must independently satisfy the qualification requirements of IRC Section 41(d) without taking into account activities relating to the development of the product itself. Every expenditure claimed on Form 6765 must be traceable to a distinct qualifying business component, must be eligible to be treated as a research or experimental expenditure under IRC Section 174 (or IRC Section 174A for tax years beginning after December 31, 2024, following the enactment of Public Law 119-21), and must satisfy the strict statutory definitions governing in-house research expenses and contract research expenses under IRC Section 41(b) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2.
Categories of Qualified Research Expenses (Section F and Section G)

The Instructions for Form 6765 require taxpayers to segregate QREs into four distinct statutory expense categories—plus basic research payments where applicable—that populate Section G (Columns 50 through 56) when Section G is completed and summarize into Section F (Lines 42 through 48). The primary expenditure category for most claimants is in-house qualified wages under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(A)(i), which encompasses wages (as defined in IRC Section 3401(a) for income tax withholding purposes, subject to special rules for self-employed individuals under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(D)) paid or incurred for an employee in the performance of "qualified services". Importantly, under the flush language of IRC Section 41(b)(2)(A) and the explicit instructions for Section F, Line 42, qualified wages cannot include any amount of wages taken into account in computing the Work Opportunity Credit under IRC Section 51 (reported on Form 5884).

When Section G is completed, the Form 6765 instructions require taxpayers to disaggregate in-house qualified wages for each reported business component into three functional subcategories across Columns 50, 51, and 52, which are then summed in Column 53 (Total Qualified Wages) and carried in aggregate to Section F, Line 42. Column 50 captures the direct conduct of qualified research under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(B)(i) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(c)(1), representing bench scientists, design engineers, metallurgists, or software developers directly executing laboratory experimentation, mathematical modeling, simulation, or prototype fabrication and testing. Column 51 captures the direct supervision of qualified research under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(B)(ii) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(c)(2), encompassing first-line technical managers (such as a senior research scientist or lead engineering manager) who directly supervise experimental trials while strictly excluding higher-level managers or corporate executives to whom first-line research managers report, even if those higher-level executives are themselves qualified scientists or engineers. Column 52 captures the direct support of qualified research under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(B)(iii) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(c)(3), covering technical and support staff who directly support individuals engaging in or directly supervising qualified research—such as a machinist machining a part of an experimental model, a laboratory worker cleaning equipment used in qualified research, a clerk compiling research test data, or a secretary typing reports describing laboratory results derived from qualified research. Conversely, Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(c)(3) strictly excludes general and administrative services that only indirectly benefit research activities, regardless of whether the personnel are assigned to an R&D department, including payroll personnel preparing salary checks for laboratory scientists, accountants accounting for research expenses, janitors performing general cleaning of a research laboratory, or corporate officers supervising financial or personnel matters. When an employee performs both qualified and non-qualified services during the taxable year, Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(d)(1) requires multiplying the employee's total statutory wages by the ratio of the time spent performing qualified services to the total time spent performing all services. However, under the "substantially all" rule of IRC Section 41(b)(2)(B), Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(d)(2), and the Form 6765 instructions, if at least 80% of the services performed by an employee for the taxpayer during the taxable year constitute qualified services, then 100% of that employee's statutory wages for the taxable year may be treated as qualified wages.

Beyond employee compensation, the Form 6765 instructions govern three non-wage expenditure categories and basic research payments. Under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(A)(ii) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(b)(1)–(2), qualified supplies (reported in Column 54 of Section G and summarized on Line 43 of Section F) include any tangible property other than land or improvements to land, and any property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation, that is directly used and consumed in the performance of qualified services. Consequently, raw materials, chemicals, electronic components, and alloys consumed in fabricating and destructively testing experimental prototypes qualify as supply QREs, whereas indirect research expenditures, general and administrative office supplies, travel, meals, shipping, training, or capitalizable depreciable laboratory equipment are strictly excluded. With respect to utility charges (water, electricity, and natural gas), Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(b)(2) treats general building utilities (such as general laboratory lighting) as excluded general and administrative expenses, but permits an exception for "extraordinary expenditures" to the extent the taxpayer establishes that the special character of the qualified research (such as operating high-energy laser or nuclear research equipment) required additional extraordinary utility consumption.

Under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(A)(iii) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(b)(4), rental or lease costs of computers (reported in Column 55 of Section G and summarized on Line 44 of Section F) provide a narrow statutory exception to the general post-1985 rule disallowing payments for the use of personal property. Under the explicit instructions for Line 44 and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(b)(4), amounts paid or incurred to another person for the right to use time-sharing computers in the conduct of qualified research qualify only if the computer is owned and operated by someone other than the taxpayer, is located off the taxpayer's premises, and the taxpayer is not the operator or primary user of the computer (and the claimed amount must be reduced by any amount received or accrued by the taxpayer for the right to use substantially identical property). In modern engineering workflows, this category encompasses eligible third-party cloud-computing server hosting costs dedicated directly to development, simulation, and testing environments rather than commercial production hosting.

Finally, under the general rule of IRC Section 41(b)(3)(A) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(e)(1), contract research expenses (reported in Column 56 of Section G and summarized on Line 45 of Section F) allow the claimant to include 65% of any amount paid or incurred to any person other than an employee of the taxpayer for qualified research performed on the taxpayer's behalf. The statutory inclusion rate increases to 75% for payments to qualified research consortia under IRC Section 41(b)(3)(C) and 100% for eligible energy research payments conducted by an eligible small business, university, or federal laboratory under IRC Section 41(b)(3)(D). Per Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(e)(1)–(3) and the Form 6765 instructions, third-party contract costs qualify only if the agreement is entered into prior to the performance of the qualified research, the agreement provides that the research be performed on behalf of the taxpayer, the taxpayer retains substantial rights to the research results, and the taxpayer bears the economic risk of the development such that the taxpayer must pay for the research even if it is not successful. If any payment is contingent upon the success of the research, Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(e)(2) disqualifies the expenditure as a payment for a finished product or result rather than the performance of research. Additionally, under IRC Section 41(b)(3)(B) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(e)(4), prepaid contract research expenses attributable to research conducted after the close of the taxable year are treated as paid or incurred during the subsequent taxable year in which the research is actually performed. On Section F of Form 6765, Line 45 captures total applicable contract research expenses (excluding basic research payments), Line 46 captures applicable basic research payments to qualified organizations under IRC Section 41(e), Line 47 adds Lines 45 and 46, and Line 48 adds Lines 42, 43, 44, and 47 to establish Total Qualified Research Expenses.
Section-by-Section Analysis of the 2024 Form 6765 Instructions
Section E: Mandatory "Other Information" Disclosures

Even when a taxpayer elects not to complete optional Section G for the 2024 tax year (or 2025 tax year under the extended transition rule), the Instructions for Form 6765 require every claimant reporting QREs on Section F, Line 48 to complete Section E (Lines 37 through 41). Crucially, under the IRS post-release clarification issued on June 18, 2025, if the claimant is a member of a controlled group filing a separate tax return, Section E must be completed strictly for the filing member's own QREs reported in Section F rather than the combined controlled group QREs. Section E acts as an automated screening mechanism on the face of the return, capturing five critical risk indicators that previously required an examiner to open an audit and issue an initial IDR.

Line 37 requires the taxpayer to report the exact total number of business components generating the QREs reported on Line 5 (Section A) or Line 20 (Section B), which equal Line 48 of Section F. Consequently, even without listing each component in Section G in 2024—or when itemizing only the top components reaching 80% of QREs (up to 50 components) in Section G—the taxpayer must establish and report on Line 37 the complete count of all qualifying business components that sum to 100% of Line 48 QREs prior to filing. Line 38 requires the exact dollar amount of corporate officers' wages included in total qualified wages on Section F, Line 42. Under the Form 6765 instructions, a corporation determines who qualifies as an officer under the laws of the state of incorporation (and an officer's status as a shareholder does not alter this reporting requirement). Because executive compensation is a frequent area of examination adjustment under Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(c)(2)–(3) (which excludes supervision above first-line management and officers supervising financial or personnel matters), isolating officers' wages on Line 38 enables immediate IRS ratio screening.

Line 39 captures a binary ("Yes"/"No") indicator of whether the taxpayer acquired or disposed of any major portion of a trade or business during the tax year, which directly triggers base-period adjustment verification under the mandatory acquisition and disposition rules of IRC Section 41(f)(3). Line 40 requires a binary ("Yes"/"No") disclosure of whether the taxpayer included any new categories of expenditures as current-year QREs compared to prior filings, alerting examiners to methodology expansions and triggering base-period consistency scrutiny under IRC Section 41(c)(5) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-3(d) (or 3-year lookback consistency under Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-9(c)(2)). Finally, Line 41 records a binary ("Yes"/"No") indicator of whether any portion of the QREs reported on Line 5 or Line 20 was determined following the LB&I ASC 730 Financial Statement R&D Directive (LB&I-04-0917-005, applicable to LB&I taxpayers with assets equal to or greater than $10,000,000 that prepare U.S. GAAP Certified Audited Financial Statements). If the taxpayer checks "Yes" on Line 41, the taxpayer must enter the exact dollar amount of Adjusted ASC 730 Financial Statement R&D from Appendix C, Line 19 (which must equal Column A total of Appendix B) on Line 41 and attach Appendices A, B, C, and D (Form6765ASC730AppendixA.pdf through Form6765ASC730AppendixD.pdf).
Section G: Business Component Reporting and the 80%/Top 50 Rule

Section G of the revised Form 6765 (Columns 49(a) through 56) operationalizes the IRS requirement that QREs be identified and quantified at the individual business component level. Under the Form 6765 instructions, when Section G is required (or voluntarily completed during the transition period), the taxpayer must complete Section G before completing Section F so that the column totals from Section G flow directly into Section F. Conversely, if the taxpayer is not required to complete Section G (and chooses not to do so), the taxpayer checks "No" on Question A at the top of Section F ("Are you required to complete Section G?") and enters its QREs directly on Lines 42 through 48 of Section F. Under the post-transition rules, a taxpayer is exempt from completing Section G on an original return if the taxpayer is a Qualified Small Business (QSB) electing to claim a reduced payroll tax credit in Section D, or if the taxpayer's total QREs determined at the controlled group level on Line 48 are equal to or less than $1.5 million and its average annual gross receipts for the prior 3 tax years are equal to or less than $50 million as determined under IRC Section 448(c)(3) (without regard to subparagraph (A) thereof), and the taxpayer is reporting a research credit on an original return.

For all filers completing Section G, the instructions establish the exact mechanics of the "80%/Top 50" reporting rule. Under this framework, taxpayers must first quantify QREs by business component and rank all qualifying business components in descending order based on the total QREs attributable to each component. From that ranked list, the taxpayer must report itemized component-by-component rows in Section G (completing Columns 49(a) through 49(e)—and Column 49(f) if filing an amended return—along with expenditure Columns 50 through 56) covering at least 80% of total QREs reported on Line 48, up to a maximum ceiling of 50 business components. If a taxpayer reaches 50 business components before reaching 80% of total QREs, itemized reporting stops at the 50th business component; conversely, if fewer than 50 business components (for example, 5 or 12 components) account for 80% or more of total QREs, the taxpayer itemizes only those components needed to reach the 80% threshold. Any remaining business components beyond the 80% threshold or beyond the 50th business component are combined into a single summary row in which the taxpayer enters "Aggregate Business Components" in Column 49(c), leaves Columns 49(a), 49(b), 49(d), 49(e), and 49(f) blank, and reports the summed residual expenditures across Columns 50 through 56. The column totals from Section G, inclusive of the "Aggregate Business Components" row, flow directly into Section F (Lines 42 through 48), ensuring strict mathematical reconciliation between project-level disclosures and total entity QREs.

Furthermore, if a taxpayer checked "Yes" on Line 41 to follow the LB&I ASC 730 Directive, the instructions direct the taxpayer to make a single entry in Section G by entering "ASC 730 Directive" in Column 49(c) and reporting the applicable Adjusted ASC 730 amounts from Appendix B (Column A only) in Columns 53, 54, 55, and 56. If that single "ASC 730 Directive" entry accounts for at least 80% of total Line 48 QREs, no additional individual business components need to be itemized (any residual QREs are entered on the "Aggregate Business Components" line); otherwise, the taxpayer must itemize additional non-Directive business components in descending order until the 80%/Top 50 threshold is satisfied. Similarly, taxpayers using statistical sampling procedures under Revenue Procedure 2011-42 must still report the 80%/Top 50 business components in Section G based on descending QRE size regardless of which components were included in the statistical sample, and must attach their sampling plan (Form6765StatSamplePlan.pdf).

For each itemized business component in Section G, Columns 49(a) through 49(f) require specific qualitative metadata. Column 49(a) captures the Employer Identification Number (EIN) of the controlled group member conducting the research activities on that business component, and Column 49(b) captures that controlled group member's Principal Business Activity (PBA) code. Column 49(c) records the business component's name or unique alphanumeric identifier, while Column 49(d) classifies the business component type (1. Product, 2. Process, or 3. All Others covering computer software, technique, formula, or invention). If the component is software, Column 49(e) requires selecting the regulatory software category (A. Internal Use Software [IUS], B. Dual Function Software [DFS], C. Non-IUS, or D. Excepted from IUS Treatment). Column 49(f) requires describing "the information sought to be discovered", which the Form 6765 instructions specify is not required on timely filed original returns (including extensions), but is mandatory when claiming a refund or credit on an amended return (or administrative adjustment request) that includes a Section 41 credit not reported on the original return or increased from the original return.

In the official Form 6765 (Rev. December 2024) and its January 2025 Instructions, Line 48 in Section F represents Total Qualified Research Expenses (summarizing Line 42 total qualified wages, Line 43 total supplies, Line 44 total computer rental or lease costs, and Line 47 total contract and basic research expenses), whereas Columns 50, 51, and 52 in Section G represent the three wage subcategories (direct conduct, direct supervision, and direct support, summed in Column 53 Total Qualified Wages), followed by Column 54 (cost of supplies), Column 55 (rental or lease cost of computers), and Column 56 (applicable amount of contract research expenses).
Hypothetical Worked Example 1: Applying the Section G 80%/Top 50 Rule and Section F Reconciliation

To illustrate the exact mathematical application of the Section G and Section F instructions on Form 6765 (Rev. December 2024 / Instructions Rev. January 2025), consider a hypothetical domestic manufacturing corporation (not in a controlled group and incurring $0 in basic research payments) claiming total QREs of $2,000,000 across 14 distinct R&D projects (business components) during the tax year. In the first phase of compliance, the taxpayer computes QREs per business component—separating direct wages (Column 50), supervision wages (Column 51), support wages (Column 52), total qualified wages (Column 53), supplies (Column 54), computer leasing (Column 55), and 65% of eligible third-party contractor payments (Column 56)—and ranks all 14 components in descending order from largest to smallest QRE total.

In this hypothetical ranking, Component BC-01 incurs $300,000 in direct wages, $50,000 in supervision wages, and $25,000 in support wages (yielding Total Qualified Wages in Column 53 of $375,000), plus $65,000 in qualified supplies (Column 54), $0 in computer leasing (Column 55), and $65,000 in contract research QREs in Column 56 (derived from 65% of gross contractor expenditures of $100,000), resulting in $505,000 of total QREs (25.25% of total QREs; cumulative 25.25% or $505,000). Component BC-02 incurs $250,000 in direct wages, $40,000 in supervision wages, and $20,000 in support wages (Total Qualified Wages in Column 53 of $310,000), plus $50,000 in supplies (Column 54), $0 in computer leasing (Column 55), and $45,500 in contract research QREs in Column 56 (gross contractor spend of $70,000), totaling $405,500 (20.275% of total QREs; cumulative 45.525% or $910,500). Component BC-03 incurs $200,000 in direct wages, $30,000 in supervision wages, and $15,000 in support wages (Total Qualified Wages in Column 53 of $245,000), plus $40,000 in supplies (Column 54), $0 in computer leasing (Column 55), and $39,000 in contract research QREs in Column 56 (gross contractor spend of $60,000), totaling $324,000 (16.20% of total QREs; cumulative 61.725% or $1,234,500). Component BC-04 incurs $150,000 in direct wages, $25,000 in supervision wages, and $10,000 in support wages (Total Qualified Wages in Column 53 of $185,000), plus $30,000 in supplies (Column 54), $0 in computer leasing (Column 55), and $26,000 in contract research QREs in Column 56 (gross contractor spend of $40,000), totaling $241,000 (12.05% of total QREs; cumulative 73.775% or $1,475,500). Component BC-05 incurs $100,000 in direct wages, $20,000 in supervision wages, and $10,000 in support wages (Total Qualified Wages in Column 53 of $130,000), plus $23,000 in supplies (Column 54), $0 in computer leasing (Column 55), and $11,500 in contract research QREs in Column 56 (gross contractor spend of $17,692.31), totaling $164,500 (8.225% of total QREs; cumulative 82.00% or $1,640,000). Finally, the remaining 9 smaller components (BC-06 through BC-14) account for combined QREs of $360,000 (18.00% of total QREs), consisting of $200,000 in direct wages, $35,000 in supervision wages, $20,000 in support wages (Total Qualified Wages in Column 53 of $255,000), $50,000 in supplies (Column 54), $0 in computer leasing (Column 55), and $55,000 in 65% contract research QREs in Column 56 (gross contractor spend of $84,615.38).
To determine the exact itemization cutoff under the 80%/Top 50 rule, the taxpayer evaluates cumulative QREs after the fourth ranked component:

Because $1,475,500 (73.775%) falls short of the mandatory 80% threshold ($1,600,000), stopping itemization at four components would violate the Section G instructions. The taxpayer must therefore also itemize the fifth ranked component, BC-05 ($164,500), bringing cumulative itemized QREs to:

At 5 business components, the taxpayer satisfies the 80% minimum threshold ($1,640,000 ≥ $1,600,000, or 82.0% ≥ 80.0%) while remaining well below the 50-component ceiling. Consequently, the remaining 9 business components (BC-06 through BC-14, totaling $360,000 or 18.0% of QREs) are consolidated onto a single line in Section G with "Aggregate Business Components" entered in Column 49(c) (leaving Columns 49(a), 49(b), 49(d), 49(e), and 49(f) blank). However, on Section E, Line 37, the taxpayer still reports the complete count of 14 total business components generating QREs.

body.text: Credit Calculation Elections on Form 6765: Sections A, B, D, and IRC Section 280C
Section A (Regular Credit) vs. Section B (Alternative Simplified Credit)

Form 6765 requires the claimant to compute the research credit under either the Regular Credit method in Section A (Lines 1 through 13) or the Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) method in Section B (Lines 14 through 26). Under Section A, governed by IRC Section 41(a)(1) and IRC Section 41(c), the Regular Credit equals 20% of the amount by which current-year QREs (reported on Section F, Line 48 and entered on Section A, Line 5) exceed the statutory base amount, plus 20% of basic research payments exceeding the qualified organization base period amount (Lines 2 through 4) and 20% of energy consortia payments (Line 1). The tentative base amount (Line 8) is computed by multiplying the taxpayer's fixed-base percentage on Line 6 (determined from historical 1984–1988 QRE and gross receipts ratios under IRC Section 41(c)(3)(A) or the start-up company rules under IRC Section 41(c)(3)(B), up to a statutory maximum cap of 16% [0.16] under IRC Section 41(c)(3)(C)) by the average annual gross receipts of the taxpayer on Line 7 for the 4 tax years preceding the credit year. Subtracting the tentative base amount (Line 8) from current-year QREs (Line 5) yields excess QREs on Line 9, which is subject to the overarching statutory floor under IRC Section 41(c)(2) providing that the base amount can never be less than 50% of current-year QREs (operationalized on Line 10 by multiplying Line 5 by 50% [0.50] and entering the smaller of Line 9 or Line 10 on Line 11). Crucially, taxpayers claiming the Regular Credit must satisfy the Consistency Rule under IRC Section 41(c)(5) (formerly designated IRC Section 41(c)(6) prior to the Tax Technical Corrections Act of 2018, Pub. L. 115-141, and still referenced as Section 41(c)(6) in Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-9(c)(2)) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-3(d), which mandates that the QREs and gross receipts taken into account in computing the fixed-base percentage for the historical base period be determined on a basis strictly consistent with the determination of QREs and gross receipts for the current credit year, regardless of whether the statute of limitations has expired for those historical base years. Inconsistencies between historical base-period definitions and current-year QRE calculations represent a primary algorithmic and examination flag for the IRS.

By contrast, under Section B, governed by IRC Section 41(c)(4) (formerly designated IRC Section 41(c)(5) prior to Pub. L. 115-141, and referenced as Section 41(c)(5) in Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-9), the Alternative Simplified Credit equals 14% of the amount by which current-year QREs (entered on Line 20 from Line 48) exceed 50% of the average QREs for the 3 preceding tax years, or 6% of current-year QREs if the taxpayer had no QREs in any one of the 3 preceding tax years. On Form 6765 (Rev. December 2024), the taxpayer enters its total QREs for the prior 3 tax years on Line 21, divides Line 21 by 6.0 on Line 22 (since dividing the 3-year sum by 3 to obtain the annual average and multiplying by 50% is mathematically identical to dividing the 3-year sum by 6.0), subtracts Line 22 from Line 20 on Line 23, and multiplies Line 23 by 14% (0.14) on Line 24 (or skips Lines 22 and 23 and multiplies Line 20 by 6% [0.06] if the taxpayer had zero QREs in any one of the prior 3 tax years). Because the ASC relies exclusively on a rolling 3-year lookback of QREs rather than historical gross receipts and 1984–1988 or start-up fixed-base percentages, it avoids multi-decade historical base-period documentation vulnerabilities, although Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-9(c)(2) still requires the prior 3 years' QREs to be determined consistently with the credit year. Under the IRS post-release clarification issued on June 18, 2025, a member of a controlled group filing a separate return enters only its own current-year QREs on Line 20 (and Line 5), whereas Line 21 requires entering the total amount of the controlled group's QREs for the prior 3 tax years, with the member's share of the group credit calculated on the required Item B attachment.

While an ASC election (or Regular Credit claim) made on an original return cannot subsequently be revoked or switched on an amended return, under final Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-9(b)(2) and the Instructions for Form 6765 ("Electing the ASC"), a taxpayer may make an initial ASC election on an amended return for a tax year provided that the taxpayer (and all members of its controlled group) did not previously claim the Section 41 credit on an original or amended return for that tax year and the assessment limitation period under IRC Section 6501(a) remains open. By contrast, the IRC Section 280C(c) reduced credit election (Header Item A) is strictly restricted by statute to the original timely filed return (including extensions). Those multipliers are simplified illustrative approximations rather than statutory tax rates: a 10% effective gross Regular Credit occurs only when the statutory 50% minimum base floor on Line 10 binds (QREs × 50% × 20% = 10% of QREs), while the statutory gross ASC formula on Line 24 is 14% of current QREs exceeding 50% of the prior 3-year average (which equals 7.0% of current QREs when current QREs equal the 3-year average: (QREs - 0.50 × QREs) × 14% = 7.0% of QREs).
The IRC Section 280C(c) Reduced Credit Election and Section D Payroll Tax Offset

Under IRC Section 280C(c)(1), a taxpayer claiming the full research credit must reduce its otherwise allowable domestic research and experimental expenditures (or the amount chargeable to capital account under IRC Section 174 for the 2024 tax year prior to the post-2024 IRC Section 174A amendments enacted in Public Law 119-21) by the amount of the gross research credit. If a taxpayer does not elect the reduced credit (by checking "No" on Header Item A), the Instructions for Form 6765 (Line 13 and Line 26) require attaching a statement (Form6765ItemASection280C.pdf) listing the deduction amounts or capitalized expenses that were reduced and identifying the return lines, schedules, or forms where the reductions were made. To avoid adjusting Section 174 amortization schedules and to simplify state tax and financial accounting computations, IRC Section 280C(c)(2) permits the taxpayer to elect a reduced research credit directly on Form 6765.

While prior versions of Form 6765 placed the Section 280C election on Lines 17 and 34, Form 6765 (Rev. December 2024) relocated the binary election to the top header of Page 1 at Item A ("Are you electing the reduced credit under section 280C? Yes / No"), and applies the mathematical reduction on Line 13 in Section A and Line 26 in Section B. Under IRC Section 280C(c)(2)(B), the gross credit is reduced by the maximum corporate tax rate (21% under IRC Section 11(b)), yielding a net credit equal to 79% (100% - 21%) of the gross credit. On Line 13 of Section A, electing taxpayers multiply Line 12 directly by 15.8% (0.158, which equals 20% × 79%), whereas on Line 26 of Section B, electing taxpayers multiply Line 25 by 79% (0.79). As emphasized in IRC Section 280C(c)(2)(C) and the Form 6765 instructions, the Section 280C(c) election must be made on an original timely filed tax return (including extensions) and is strictly irrevocable for that tax year.

In Section C (Current Year Credit, Lines 27 through 32), the taxpayer reduces the credit by any overlapping employer differential wage credit from Form 8932 (Line 27), adds pass-through research credits from partnerships, S corporations, estates, and trusts (Line 29), and reports the current-year credit on Form 3800, Part III, Line 4i (for eligible small businesses with 3-year average annual gross receipts not exceeding $50,000,000) or Line 1c (for all other filers). Additionally, Section D (Lines 33a through 36) of Form 6765 allows a Qualified Small Business (QSB)—defined under IRC Section 41(h)(3) as an entity with less than $5,000,000 in gross receipts for the credit year and no gross receipts for any tax year preceding the 5-tax-year period ending with the credit year (aggregated across controlled group members)—to elect on Box 33a (and Box 33b if payroll tax is reported under a different EIN) to apply up to $500,000 of its research credit (entered on Line 34 and finalized on Line 36) against employer payroll tax liabilities via Form 8974.

Substantive Qualification: The Four-Part Test and Statutory Exclusions
Component-by-Component Application of the Four-Part Test (IRC Section 41(d))

The Instructions for Form 6765 and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4(b)(1) explicitly mandate that the statutory Four-Part Test under IRC Section 41(d)(1) be applied separately with respect to each business component of the taxpayer. Under the "shrinking-back" rule of Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4(b)(2) and the Form 6765 instructions, if a complete product or process fails to satisfy the Four-Part Test as a whole, the test is applied at the most significant subset of elements—such as a subassembly, subsystem, compressor blade, or software module—that does satisfy all four statutory criteria, continuing until either a qualifying subset of elements is reached or the most basic element of the product fails to qualify. Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4(b)(2) emphasizes that the shrinking-back rule applies only when the overall business component fails to meet IRC Section 41(d)(1) and may not itself be used as a reason to exclude research activities when the overall product satisfies the requirements (as illustrated in Trinity Industries, Inc. v. United States, 757 F.3d 400 (5th Cir. 2014)).

Activity must intend to develop a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality of a business component; cosmetic, style, taste, or seasonal design changes are excluded.

Architectural diagrams, chemical formulas, mechanical CAD models, or computer science algorithms.

4. Process of Experimentation

Substantially all (80% or more) of the research activities for each business component must constitute elements of a structured evaluative process capable of testing one or more alternatives via modeling, simulation, or systematic trial and error.
Hypothesis-test-conclusion logs, failed prototype test reports, simulation runs, and iterative design logs.
Contemporaneous employee time-tracking (wages) and material consumption logs (supplies) tied to trials.

body.text: Statutory Exclusions Under IRC Section 41(d)(4)

Even where technical work involves engineering or computer science personnel, IRC Section 41(d)(4), Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4(c), and the Form 6765 instructions strictly exclude eight specific categories of activity from qualifying as research. First, under IRC Section 41(d)(4)(A) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4(c)(2), any activity conducted after the beginning of commercial production of the business component—when the component is ready for commercial sale or use or meets the taxpayer's basic functional and economic requirements—is statutorily ineligible, including preproduction planning, tooling-up for production, trial production runs, and troubleshooting faults in production equipment. Second, under IRC Section 41(d)(4)(B) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4(c)(3), activities aimed at adapting an existing business component to a particular customer's requirement or need are excluded. Third, under IRC Section 41(d)(4)(C) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4(c)(4), the statute bars the duplication or reverse engineering of an existing business component (in whole or in part) from a physical examination of the component itself or from plans, blueprints, detailed specifications, or publicly available information.

Fourth, under IRC Section 41(d)(4)(D) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4(c)(5), routine business operations—including efficiency surveys, activities relating to management function or technique, market research, testing, or development (including advertising or promotions), routine quality control testing or inspection, and routine data collection—are excluded. Fifth, under IRC Section 41(d)(4)(F) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4(c)(7), any research conducted outside the United States, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, or any territory or possession of the United States is ineligible for the credit, requiring apportionment when services are performed both inside and outside the United States. Sixth, under IRC Section 41(d)(4)(G) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4(c)(8), research in the social sciences, arts, or humanities is excluded.

Seventh, under IRC Section 41(d)(4)(E) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4(c)(6), with respect to computer software developed by or for the benefit of the taxpayer primarily for internal use in general and administrative (G&A) functions (financial management, human resource management, and support services)—which must be categorized in Section G, Column 49(e) of the revised Form 6765—costs are excluded unless the software is developed to be commercially sold, leased, licensed, or marketed to third parties or to interact with third parties (Non-IUS, Option C), is used in an activity that constitutes qualified research or in a production process that meets the Four-Part Test (Excepted from IUS Treatment, Option D), or satisfies the rigorous three-part High Threshold of Innovation (HTI) test under Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii) (applicable to IUS, Option A, and the 25% safe harbor for Dual Function Software [DFS], Option B). To pass the HTI test, the taxpayer must establish that: (1) the software is innovative, resulting in a substantial and economically significant reduction in cost, improvement in speed, or other measurable improvement; (2) the software development involves significant economic risk, where the taxpayer commits substantial resources and there is substantial uncertainty, because of technical risk, that those resources would be recovered within a reasonable period; and (3) the software is not commercially available for use by the taxpayer without modifications that themselves satisfy the first two HTI requirements. Eighth, under IRC Section 41(d)(4)(H) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4(c)(9), any research to the extent funded by any grant, contract, or otherwise by another person or governmental entity is excluded whenever the taxpayer performing the research does not retain substantial rights in the research results or does not bear the financial risk of development failure.
IRS Examination Risk Triggers, Notice 2002-44, and Substantiation Architecture
Automated Screening and Comparative QRE Analysis
Examination selection for Form 6765 claims combines automated statistical screening with targeted examiner review.

Under the IRS Audit Techniques Guide (ATG): Credit for Increasing Research Activities (IRC § 41) (Determining the Scope), examiners begin their risk assessment by executing a multi-year comparative spreadsheet analysis of QREs reported on Form 6765, evaluating wages, supplies, computer leasing, and contract research expenses against prior and subsequent tax years in the context of the taxpayer's overall business operations. Unexplained spikes in total QREs on Line 48, shifts in the ratio of supplies (Line 43) or contractor costs (Line 45) to wages (Line 42), high officer wage disclosures on Section E (Line 38), unadjusted M&A events on Line 39, or newly added QRE expense categories on Line 40 immediately flag the return for in-depth examination.
The "Prepackaged Submission" Trap and Contemporaneous Nexus

The most pervasive cause of credit disallowance during an IRS examination is the failure to establish nexus—the verifiable accounting and technical bridge connecting specific QRE dollars (employee hours, consumed prototype supplies, leased developmental computers, and contractor invoices) to specific experimental activities performed on an identified business component. Both the general IRS Audit Techniques Guide (IRC § 41) and the Research Credit Claims Audit Techniques Guide (RCCATG) explicitly warn examiners against relying on generic, retrospective "prepackaged submissions" (often delivered in multi-binder studies prepared by third-party consultants) that emphasize general estimation methodologies while failing to substantiate with competent evidence that the taxpayer actually paid or incurred QREs for qualified activities.

Crucially, the IRS ATGs note that audit adjustments grounded solely on an examiner's critique of a taxpayer's general estimation methodology—without developing the underlying factual record—are difficult for the IRS to sustain in Appeals or litigation. Consequently, IRS examiners are instructed to bypass boilerplate consultant narratives, reject unsupported departmental cost-center estimates or non-statistical judgment samples, and issue IDRs or summonses demanding primary source records. Under the ATG, routine IDR requests include the general ledger chart of accounts, QRE accounting procedures, reconciliation workpapers bridging the general ledger to Form 6765, all back-up workpapers and risk/exposure analyses retained by the third-party study provider, contemporaneous project test logs, and—where employee surveys, questionnaires, or interviews were used—copies of the survey instruments, instructions, timestamps, and underlying responses. Furthermore, oral testimony or retrospective interviews conducted months or years after the tax year without corroborating contemporaneous documentation (as required under Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4(d) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.6001-1, enforceable via a Notice of Inadequate Records under Treasury Regulation Section 1.6001-1(d)) are routinely rejected under judicial precedents such as Eustace v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2001-66, aff'd, 312 F.3d 905 (7th Cir. 2002).
Procedural Completeness and Notice 2002-44 / Refund Claim Specificity

Procedural defects on Form 6765 create immediate administrative exposure even when underlying R&D activities are technically sound. The IRS ATG instructs examiners that if Form 6765 is not properly completed in accordance with its instructions—which includes completing Header Items A and B, mandatory Section E, and mandatory Section F in 2024, and Section G once mandatory—the examiner must require the taxpayer to cure the deficiencies and provide the relevant information before accepting or examining the claim.

For claims for credit or refund on amended returns, the administrative rules evolved through three distinct stages that must be precisely distinguished. First, under Notice 2002-44, 2002-2 C.B. 39 (cited in the 2005 IRS Audit Techniques Guide), corporate Form 1120 research credit refund claims were directed to the Ogden Service Center (with a separate procedure for certain taxpayers under audit to submit claims to the LMSB/SBSE manager) and were required to include a completed Form 6765, set forth in detail each ground upon which the credit was claimed, provide facts sufficient to apprise the IRS of the exact basis of the claim under Treasury Regulation Section 301.6402-2(b)(1), and be verified under penalties of perjury. Second, in Notice 2008-39, 2008-13 I.R.B. 684 (reflected in the RCCATG and Form 6765 instructions), the IRS explicitly superseded Notice 2002-44, eliminating the procedure allowing taxpayers under examination to submit research credit claims directly to IRS auditors and requiring paper corporate refund claims to be filed on a formal amended return at the Ogden Service Center labeled "Refund-Research Credit" with both the original Form 6765 (if any) and an amended Form 6765 attached.

Third, under IRS Chief Counsel Memorandum (CCM) 20214101F (effective January 10, 2022) as streamlined by the IRS on June 18, 2024, and integrated into the Instructions for Form 6765 (Rev. January 2025, "Research Credit Claims on Amended Returns"), a taxpayer filing an amended return (or administrative adjustment request [AAR]) claiming a new or increased Section 41 credit must provide upfront: (1) identification of all business components to which the Section 41 claim relates for that tax year; (2) for each business component, identification of all research activities performed and—by completing Section G, Column 49(f) of the revised Form 6765—a description of "the information sought to be discovered"; and (3) the total qualified employee wage expenses, supply expenses, computer rental/lease expenses, and contract research expenses for the claim year (which may be satisfied using Form 6765). In its June 18, 2024 FAQ update, the IRS waived the upfront requirement to list the specific names or job titles of the individuals who performed each research activity (former Item 3) and the information each individual sought to discover (former Item 4) on the initial amended return submission, reserving employee-specific requests for substantive examination. During the IRS transition period (extended through January 10, 2027), taxpayers notified of a deficient refund claim via Letter 6426C or Letter 6428 are granted 45 days to perfect the claim via paper mail or fax (portable electronic storage devices are not accepted), after which unperfected claims are rejected without Appeals rights.
Strategic Compliance Synthesis for 2024 and 2025 Filers

The 2024 Form 6765 instructions mark a decisive transition in federal research credit administration. Even though Section G remains optional for 2024 original tax returns (and through 2025 under the extended transition period prior to mandatory enforcement for tax years beginning after 2025), the mandatory implementation of Header Items A and B, Section E (Lines 37–41), and Section F (Lines 42–48) in 2024—followed by the mandatory enforcement of Section G's 80%/Top 50 business component reporting—requires taxpayers to treat the 2024–2025 filing cycles as an operational dry run.

To ensure full compliance with the revised Form 6765 instructions and insulate claims from IRS examination adjustments, taxpayers and tax professionals must execute four structural actions across their accounting and technical workflows. First, organizations must reconfigure cost accounting around discrete business components so that general ledger chart-of-account structures and engineering time-tracking systems map directly to individual project identifiers (Column 49(c)), component types (Column 49(d)), and software classifications (Column 49(e)) rather than broad departmental cost centers, separating wages into direct conduct (Column 50), direct supervision (Column 51), and direct support (Column 52) while isolating corporate officers' wages on Section E, Line 38. Second, claimants must enforce contemporaneous technical substantiation by time-stamping technical unknowns and iterative hypothesis-testing logs during the tax year as experimentation occurs, establishing an auditable nexus between each business component's technical Four-Part Test narrative and its Section G expenditure columns (and completing Column 49(f) for any amended return refund claim). Third, before selecting Section A (Regular Credit) or Section B (ASC), claimants must audit base-period consistency under IRC Section 41(c)(5) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-3(d) (or 3-year lookback consistency under Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-9(c)(2)), apply the June 18, 2025 IRS clarification for separate-filing controlled group members in Sections E and F and on Lines 5 and 20, and verify that officers' wages (Line 38), business acquisitions or dispositions (Line 39), new QRE categories (Line 40), ASC 730 Directive amounts (Line 41), and total business component counts (Line 37) in Section E reconcile precisely with underlying workpapers. Finally, because the IRC Section 280C(c) reduced credit election—made on Header Item A on Page 1 and calculated on Line 13 (at 15.8%) or Line 26 (at 79%)—is strictly irrevocable and can only be made on an original timely filed return (including extensions), taxpayers must model the net tax impact of Section 280C(c) alongside IRC Section 174 (and post-2024 IRC Section 174A) capitalization and amortization schedules prior to filing the original 2024 return.
